drug_class: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (a type of immunotherapy / cancer medicine)
purpose: Nivolumab is used to treat several types of cancer, including certain lung cancers, skin cancer (melanoma), kidney cancer, bladder cancer, and others. It helps your immune system find and fight cancer cells more effectively. Your doctor chose this medicine because it can slow or stop cancer from growing.
how_it_works: Your immune system has natural 'brakes' that stop it from attacking your own body. Cancer cells can hijack these brakes to hide from your immune system. Nivolumab blocks one of those brakes — called PD-1 — so your immune system can recognize and attack the cancer cells again.
common_side_effects: Feeling very tired, skin rash or itching, diarrhea or upset stomach, nausea, decreased appetite, joint or muscle aches, and cough. Some people also notice changes in their lab tests like liver or thyroid levels.
warnings: Because this medicine revs up your immune system, it can sometimes cause it to attack healthy organs — this is called an immune-related reaction. It can affect your lungs, liver, intestines, kidneys, skin, or hormone glands. Tell your doctor or nurse RIGHT AWAY if you have severe diarrhea, trouble breathing, yellowing of the skin or eyes, severe rash, or feel very unwell. These reactions can be serious but are treatable if caught early.
typical_dosing: Nivolumab is given as an IV infusion (a drip into your vein) at a clinic or hospital, usually every 2, 4, or 6 weeks depending on your cancer type and treatment plan. Each infusion takes about 30 to 60 minutes. Your doctor will decide the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
